newsitem.title: THAILAND: Clinton witnesses signing of U.S.-Thai tax pact.
newsitem.headline: Clinton witnesses signing of U.S.-Thai tax pact.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton on Tuesday witnessed the signing of an agreement that will spare American and Thai companies being taxed twice on profits earned in both countries.
Clinton, in Thailand for a 27-hour visit, and caretaker Thai Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa observed the conclusion of a tax pact that took more than a decade to negotiate.

The treaty "opens a new era of trade and investment between Thailand and the United States... Today the doors of opportunity have been opened a little wider," Clinton said at the signing ceremony at Bangkok's Grand Palace.

"Today's signing reminds us that governments do not create wealth but governments can create the climate in which our workers, our entrepreneurs, our investors and our business people can have a free and unfettered opportunity to thrive. That is our goal with this treaty."
Thai statistics say two-way U.S.-Thai trade amounted to about $18 billion in 1995 with Thailand enjoying about $1.5 billion of trade surplus.
But Thai officials said they expected the surplus to swing to a deficit this year for the first time in a decade.

The absence of the treaty had in the past prompted American investors in Thai equities to circumvent Thai capital gains and dividend taxes by investing through holding firms in countries that have tax agreements with Bangkok, brokers said.

"As both Thailand the United States strive to deepen their economic relationship...the need to provide strong incentives to our respective private sectors to increase the level and scope of business activities...has become paramount," Banharn said after the treaty was signed.
"This agreement is therefore timely...to reduce the costs of American firms doing business in Thailand and vice versa," he said.
The tax treaty, a highlight of Clinton's visit to Thailand, was signed by Thai Foreign Minister Amnuay Viravan and U.S. Ambassador William Itoh.
